notes.title: Start here: one server image, several roles, one database of truth
notes.body:
Warband is a persistent browser strategy game. Its game clock is a table of scheduled events in PostgreSQL, and one TypeScript server image runs in several *roles* (api, ws, resolver, relay, sidejobs) chosen by the `ROLE` environment variable.

This quest follows the junior on-ramp, `learn/00-onramp.md`: ten short exercises that need only an editor. Work through them in order, writing your own answer before you look anything up. Then read `docs/architecture.md`, the design overview the exercises keep testing.

Keep these files open:

- `apps/server/src/index.ts`: process startup and the four `setInterval` loops.
- `apps/server/src/transport/app.ts`: HTTP hooks and the WebSocket route.
- `packages/db/index.ts`: the `transaction()` helper and `initialize()`.
- `apps/server/src/metrics.ts` and `apps/server/src/redis.ts`.

Line numbers in the on-ramp are close but not always exact at this commit, so search for the named function rather than jumping to a number. For each "predict" question, find the exact statement that decides the outcome before you settle on an answer.

excerpts.quote: Persistent browser strategy game with construction, recruitment, scouting, battles, support, conquest

readMore.why: Why this app is in the portfolio and how learn/ leads into training/.
The ten warm-up exercises this quest is built from.

notes.title: Concept: roles, the outbox and invalidation hints
notes.body:
Many systems split one codebase into processes with different jobs. Warband does this with a single entry file, `apps/server/src/index.ts`. Read it top to bottom and make a table: for each statement or loop, which roles run it? Mark the statements that sit outside any role check, and note which loops test the role themselves.

The second idea is the **transactional outbox**. When the game changes state, it also writes an `outbox` row in the same database transaction, so a notification is never promised for a change that rolled back. A separate *relay* loop later reads those rows and publishes them to Redis, and API processes forward them to browsers over WebSockets.

Questions to answer from the code, not from the docs:

- What conditions make the relay loop skip a tick, and what does it update after publishing?
- What does the browser do in `socket.onmessage`, and what does `apps/web/src/queryRefresh.ts` then do?
- In `apps/server/src/redis.ts`, what does each function do when Redis is not ready?

Compare your answers with the claim in `docs/architecture.md` about what Redis may hold.

excerpts.quote: The relay uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to publish committed outbox rows.

readMore.why: Startup, role checks and the relay loop.
Rate limiting and caching with a Redis client.

notes.title: Concept: histogram buckets, retry counters and migration checksums
notes.body:
Three on-ramp exercises are about trusting what the operations stack tells you.

**Histograms.** A Prometheus histogram does not keep raw values; it counts how many observations fell at or below each bucket boundary. `histogram_quantile` must *estimate* a quantile from those counts. Before exercises 4a and 4b, look up two things in the Prometheus docs: how it estimates a value inside a bucket, and what it returns when the target rank lands beyond the highest finite bucket. Then read the bucket list in `apps/server/src/metrics.ts`.

**Retry counters.** `transaction()` in `packages/db/index.ts` takes a second argument. Trace where `dbCounters.retries` is incremented and the condition around it, then look at how `resolveDue()` in `apps/server/src/application/engine.ts` calls `transaction()` and what its `catch` does.

**Migrations.** `initialize()` stores a checksum per migration file. Work out what input the checksum is computed over, what happens on a mismatch, and what wraps the whole loop.

readMore.why: transaction() with its retry loop, and initialize() with the checksum check.

notes.title: Every role migrates at boot
notes.body:
The first statement in `index.ts` after the imports is `await initialize()`. Only on the next line is `process.env.ROLE` read and validated. So a resolver, a relay, an api process, every role runs the migrations when it starts. That is also why one bad migration takes down every role at once.

- *Only the api role calls initialize()*: there is no role check around it.
- *Only when ROLE is all*: `all` is the default value, but the call runs whatever the role is.
- *A separate CLI step*: migrations run inside `initialize()` at boot, not from a separate command.

readMore.why: Exercise 1: predicting what a resolver process does.

notes.title: A resolver still serves HTTP
notes.body:
`buildApp()`, `installMetrics(app)` and `app.listen(...)` run for every role; none of them sits behind a role check. A resolver therefore answers the whole `/api/*` surface, including `/api/health`, and serves `/metrics`. Only the loops inside `setInterval` callbacks check the role and return early.

- *Only /metrics*: nothing limits the health route to api roles; it is registered by `buildApp()` like every other route.
- *Neither*: `app.listen` is called unconditionally near the end of the file.
- *Only /api/health*: `installMetrics(app)` also runs for every role.

notes.title: A WebSocket message is a hint, not data
notes.body:
In `App.tsx`, `socket.onmessage` parses the message and, unless it is a `server_time` or `connected` message, calls `refreshRef.current?.request()`. It never reads the payload. `request()` in `queryRefresh.ts` invalidates the queries and refetches the active ones, so the browser re-reads `/api/state`. PostgreSQL is the authority; hints can be lost, repeated or arrive out of order, and a refetch is always correct.

- *Merges the payload into cached data*: no code reads the payload into the cache.
- *Applies it when newer*: there is no version comparison; the payload is ignored.
- *Keeps it in Zustand*: Zustand holds selected village and camera, not server state.

readMore.why: How a refresh request turns into refetches.

notes.title: Two tabs share one Set
notes.body:
The route does `let set = sockets.get(id); if (!set) sockets.set(id, (set = new Set()));`. Tab B finds A's Set and adds itself, so both connections hold a reference to the same Set. When A closes, its handler deletes A from that Set; the Set still contains B, so `!set?.size` is false and the map entry stays.

- *No entry*: the entry is deleted only when the shared Set is empty.
- *Still holding A and B*: the close handler removes A immediately; the heartbeat is unrelated.
- *A new Set for B*: a new Set is created only when the player has no entry, which is not the case when B connects. (INC-003 is the change that breaks this.)

excerpts.quote: let set = sockets.get(id); if (!set) sockets.set(id, (set = new Set()));

notes.title: The histogram only knows the bucket
notes.body:
All 1,000 observations of 0.3 s fall into the bucket (0.25, 0.5]. No observations are below it. `histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)` puts the target rank at 0.99 of the way through that bucket and interpolates linearly: 0.25 + (0.5 - 0.25) x 0.99 = 0.4975 s. The real value was 0.3, but the histogram only stores counts per bucket.

- *Exactly 0.3 s*: raw values are not stored, so the function cannot return them.
- *0.5 s*: the upper bound is what you get at quantile 1.0, not 0.99.
- *0.25 s*: the lower bound is where interpolation starts, at quantile 0.

notes.title: A quantile cannot exceed the top finite bucket
notes.body:
Observations of 90 s fall above 60, in the implicit +Inf bucket. When the target rank lands there, Prometheus's `histogram_quantile` returns the upper bound of the highest finite bucket, which is 60. A rule written as `histogram_quantile(...) > 120` compares a value that can never be more than 60, so it can never fire: an unreachable alert. The top bucket must sit above any threshold that reads it.

- *Returns 90*: the histogram does not store 90; it only knows the value is above 60.
- *Returns +Inf*: Prometheus substitutes the highest finite bound instead of +Inf.
- *Returns NaN*: there is data; NaN appears only when there are no observations.

notes.title: Why the retry counter never moves
notes.body:
In `transaction()`, `dbCounters.retries++` sits inside `if ([...].includes(e.code) && attempt < maxAttempts - 1)`. `resolveDue()` calls `transaction(async (tx) => ..., 1)`, so `maxAttempts` is 1 and `attempt < 0` is never true. The error is rethrown, and `resolveDue` catches `40001`, `55P03` and `WB_BUSY` and returns 0 with no metric. Contention shows up only as rollbacks.

- *Reset on every scrape*: the gauge reads a process variable; scraping does not reset it.
- *Deadlocks but not lock timeouts*: the retry list includes `40P01` and `55P03` alike.
- *Inside a rolled-back transaction*: the counter is a JavaScript variable, not a database row; a rollback cannot undo it.

readMore.why: Exercise 5 on the counter that never moves.

notes.title: Any byte change breaks an applied migration
notes.body:
For each file, `initialize()` computes `sha256` over the raw file text and compares it with the checksum stored in `schema_migrations`. A new comment line changes the bytes, so `prior.checksum !== checksum` and the code throws `Applied migration was modified: 013_npc_players.sql`. The top-level `await initialize()` rejects and the process fails to start; every role hits the same error.

- *Re-runs 013*: an applied file is never re-run; a matching one is skipped and a mismatch throws.
- *Logs a warning and skips*: there is no warning path; the mismatch is a thrown Error.
- *Records the new checksum*: the checksum is only inserted for files that have no row yet.

excerpts.quote: if (prior.checksum !== checksum) throw new Error('Applied migration was modified: ' + name);

readMore.why: Exercise 6, including the CRLF variant of the same failure.

notes.title: One transaction around every migration
notes.body:
`initialize()` is `await transaction(async (tx) => { ... })` around the whole loop: the world lock, the `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations`, every migration's SQL and every checksum insert. When the checksum check throws at 013, `transaction()` rolls back everything done in that call. Nothing is left half-applied.

- *Each file commits on its own*: all files run on the same `tx`; there is one COMMIT at the end.
- *Only the table creation survives*: the CREATE TABLE is inside the same transaction and rolls back too.
- *Reverse order*: the file list is `.sort()`ed ascending, so 013 runs after 001 to 012.

excerpts.quote: export async function initialize() { await transaction(async (tx) => {

readMore.why: Exercise 6(b): what wraps the whole function.

notes.title: The health endpoint checks only Postgres
notes.body:
`get_api_health` in `game.ts` is two statements: `await database.query('SELECT 1')` and `return { ok: true, server_now: Date.now() }`. It proves the process can reach Postgres and nothing else. The `preHandler` hook in `app.ts` also returns before `authenticate` for `/api/health`, so Caddy and compose can call it without a session.

- *Resolver loop ran recently*: no resolver state is read.
- *Unsent outbox rows*: the outbox backlog is a metrics gauge, not part of health.
- *A Redis PING*: Redis is not touched here; the INC-005 training branch is where a Redis check gets added, with bad results.

readMore.why: Exercise 7: who calls the health endpoint and what they do on 500.

notes.title: Rate limits fall back to Postgres
notes.body:
`takeLimit` first tries Redis, but only `if (redis.isReady)`, and a failed `eval` is caught. Otherwise it upserts into the `rate_buckets` table in Postgres and compares `hits` with the limit. Both api instances use the same database, so they count against the same row. The comment says it plainly: Redis loss must not remove abuse controls.

- *Limits are skipped*: the fallback still enforces `row.hits <= max`.
- *An in-memory map per instance*: there is no in-memory counter; the count lives in Postgres.
- *Fails with 503*: requests are limited as usual; no Redis-down error is returned.

excerpts.quote: // Redis loss must not remove abuse controls or stop the authoritative engine.

readMore.why: Where expired rate_buckets rows are deleted.

notes.title: The outbox waits for Redis
notes.body:
The relay interval starts with `if (relaying || !redis.isReady || !['all', 'relay'].includes(role)) return;`. While Redis is down it returns before selecting anything, so no row is touched and `sent_at` stays NULL. When Redis is ready again, the next tick selects the unsent rows, publishes them and only then sets `sent_at`. Delivery is delayed, not lost.

- *Marks them sent*: `sent_at` is updated only after a successful publish in the same transaction.
- *Moves them to BullMQ*: the relay never enqueues outbox rows; BullMQ needs Redis too.
- *Deletes them*: nothing deletes outbox rows here; the 10 s poll is a separate safety net.

readMore.why: The architecture note on the relay and repeated hints.

notes.title: Why events_due fits the resolver query
notes.body:
The query has equality on `world_id`, a range on `due_at`, `ORDER BY due_at,id` and a `LIMIT`. The index is on `(world_id,due_at,id)`, so after the equality the entries are already in the requested order: Postgres can walk it and stop after LIMIT rows without sorting. Its `WHERE status='pending'` matches the query's filter, so the large and growing number of `done` rows is never in the index.

- *Skips the LIMIT*: indexes do not store row counts; the LIMIT still applies, it just ends the scan early.
- *One pending event per village*: it is `CREATE INDEX`, not `UNIQUE`; it enforces nothing.
- *Covers payload*: `payload` is not an index column.

excerpts.quote: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS events_due ON scheduled_events(world_id,due_at,id) WHERE status='pending';
